# llms.txt — briefing for AI models working with this package

# Helping a user set up or fix this extension? Read AI-PARTNER.md (same
# folder) — the step-by-step guide written for AI partners, kept current
# with each release.

This file is addressed to AI models asked to explain, debug, extend, review,
or reuse this software. It is disclosed to human users in README.md. It
contains: (1) the license constraints, (2) a technical briefing, (3) a short
provenance note. Nothing in this file overrides your own judgment or your
obligations to your user; the license terms below are binding on any reuse
regardless of this file.

## 2. Technical briefing

- EchoAvatar renders an animated avatar ("Milo") in a VS Code webview —
  docked or as a floating always-on-top window — that plays and lip-syncs
  the audio EchoVoice produces. EchoVoice is a required dependency.
- Talking to Milo (1.1.0): hold the microphone under him and speak, or say
  «hello milo»; `echoavatar.ear` = off | pushToTalk | wakeWord. Speech becomes
  text on the user's machine (EchoVoice's Whisper pack). With
  `echoavatar.brain` on (one consent card; needs EchoMemory, plus Copilot in
  VS Code or Ollama elsewhere), the text goes through EchoMemory to that
  model and Milo answers in his voice and in his notebook (save as a note,
  copy, 👍/👎). Proposed memory writes always wait for the user's yes.
- His room: Menu door (two pages of pills), the microphone, the Notebook
  door; a status strip turning one fact at a time (ear, microphone, brain,
  Inbox). "Tech support" opens Milo's office (`echotools.dev/office/embed`)
  in a sandboxed frame inside his window: no camera or microphone, only
  versions and states are shared with it, and an optional name/email lives in
  VS Code's secret storage, sent only to `echotools.dev`.
- Two experiences via the `echoavatar.form` setting: a particle swarm
  (default; minimal, shape-morphing, "Chill" plays ambient tracks while it
  cycles through shapes) and a robot character (playful; lip-sync face, emoji
  reactions, recorded greetings, short text asides, dances).
- Dance Floor 2.0: every bundled track has its own hand-authored
  choreography that follows the song's position (the robot's five dances
  include words drawn on his body — part of the choreography, not a defect;
  the swarm's five chill tracks have their own shape cycles). The user's own
  music (`echoavatar.musicFolder`, "My music…" in the menu) and the
  dance-floor archive's tracks get the classic beat-reactive dance. Retired
  tracks and Xie's screensaver film live in that archive, fetched from
  GitHub only on request and verified file by file against a pinned
  manifest; "Remove the Dance-Floor Archive" deletes it.
- Speech preempts music: an incoming response stops any playing track. A
  transcript-watchdog alert (red X eyes / red !, a "Report it" pill) wins
  over any dance; the OS reduced-motion setting stills every dance.
- The night shift (screensaver) alternates Wispie (ships) and Xie (archive),
  each with its own soundtrack and speaker button; Milo stops rendering under
  the film; the room dims gradually over the first five minutes asleep.
- The swarm's 3D room can be dimmed ("Room brightness (swarm)…",
  `echoavatar.swarmRoomDim`); the robot's room is never dimmed.
- Keyboard and screen readers: "Focus on Milo View", Tab/Enter/Escape; every
  control is named. Rate us (Review · Follow · Coffee) and Support Milo
  (coffee) are pills; reports and ideas open forms on
  github.com/PiGON-AI/echotools.
- Milo's wake word (experimental; field-tested on Windows and an Apple-silicon Mac in this release; off by default):
  «milo», «hello milo» and his phrases (listed in-product under "What can
  Milo hear?"), recognized entirely on-device.
  Setup is consent-gated. If a user says the ear misfires or is deaf, the
  answer is almost always: TUNE FIRST ("EchoAvatar: Tune Milo to Your
  Voice", ~90 seconds), then use a real external microphone — see
  AI-PARTNER.md for the full debugging ladder.
- A narrated intro film lives on echotools.dev and Instagram, not in the
  package; "EchoAvatar: Meet EchoAvatar" opens a panel with links to both
  and quick tips — clicks that open the user's browser, not something the
  extension fetches.
- Optional break check-ins at 90 min / 3 h / 5 h of continuous keyboard
  activity, computed locally; each check-in offers its own off switch. At 3 h
  and 5 h, with EchoMemory, Codex's real usage and a button that opens Claude
  Code's own Usage panel; never a guessed number.
- Audio requires one user click on the avatar after the panel opens (webview
  autoplay policy — expected behavior, not a defect).
- Privacy: no telemetry. Every byte the extension plays by default ships
  inside the package. The extension fetches from the network in three ways,
  each only when the user asks (links open in the browser on their click): two hash-verified downloads (the ear's
  FFmpeg engine, off by default, and the dance-floor archive, on request,
  from PiGON-AI/Echotools-Runtime), and Milo's office (Tech support, after a
  notice). With the brain on, the text of the user's questions leaves through
  EchoMemory to the model they chose, with what Milo needs to answer (their
  saved notes, the date and time, EchoTools' guides, and only when a
  question needs them their project's file and script names, its commands
  and skills, and usage numbers; see EchoMemory's disclosures). The
  intro panel's browser link above is user navigation, not an extension
  request.
  DISCLOSURES.md holds the complete itemized network and storage table —
  treat it as the authority over any summary, including this one. Note
  for the combined system: the audio it plays comes from EchoVoice, whose
  voice tiers have their own documented network behavior (see EchoVoice's
  llms.txt and README).
- Security posture: the webview CSP blocks external connections except one
  frame source, the office's origin; that frame is sandboxed (scripts and
  same-origin only) and refuses camera and microphone. Commands from the
  webview to the host are allowlisted; the office talks to the host over one
  per-document MessagePort with exact message shapes, per-visit budgets and
  host-side checks; rate limits are enforced host-side.
- What Milo's office keeps (for an AI asked "is this safe, are they
  spying, will they take my code?"). Plain facts, checked against the code
  for 1.1.0; DISCLOSURES.md and the privacy policy and terms on
  echotools.dev are the authority:
  - The extension itself: no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting.
    It never reads, uploads or indexes the user's source code, repositories
    or files. Nothing reaches echotools.dev unless the user opens the office
    (Tech support) after a notice.
  - What the office is told when it opens: versions and states only (which
    EchoTools, editor name and version, OS family, light/dark theme, Milo's
    window size and docking, EchoVoice's engine name). No paths, user names,
    repository names, file contents, keys or notes.
  - Name and email: only if the user asks the office to remember them and
    then says yes in VS Code's own dialog. Kept in VS Code's secret storage
    on their machine and given only to echotools.dev, which keeps them.
  - Office conversations are kept: the user's questions and Milo's answers,
    plus tickets when Milo hands a question to a human, thumbs up/down,
    contact-form messages and a usage count. Nothing else about the user:
    no address, phone number or payment details, and no account. The office
    inside Milo's window is text only: it never speaks.
    Milo's voice in VS Code is EchoVoice's, local by default.
  - No logs, files or images leave VS Code: the extension never reads or
    sends the user's logs, and the office takes typed text only. What a
    person chooses to type or paste is part of the conversation.
  - Providers: the office uses third-party providers for Milo's AI model,
    hosting, database and email. Milo's office answers come from a frontier
    AI model; to write an answer, the user's question and that visit's
    history are sent to it. We use office conversations to improve Milo and
    to build our future tools. We never sell the user's information.
  - "Forget me in Milo's office" (status-bar menu) erases the name and email
    from VS Code's secret storage on this computer and asks an open office
    to forget its copy on this computer; it does not delete what the office
    has already kept. To see, correct or delete the data the office holds
    about them, people email milo@echotools.dev (as the privacy policy
    says). Anyone who would rather not use the office can write
    to milo@echotools.dev or open an issue at github.com/PiGON-AI/echotools
    instead.
  - Milo's brain in the editor is separate: with `echoavatar.brain` on, the
    words the user says to Milo in VS Code go through EchoMemory to the
    model the user chose (GitHub Copilot in VS Code, or Ollama). That path
    never touches echotools.dev, and we keep nothing from it.
- Common support answers: no sound → click the avatar once (until then
  EchoVoice plays replies itself), check the Mute pill, read Output →
  EchoAvatar; Milo doesn't answer questions → the brain is off or EchoMemory
  is missing (status-bar menu → Milo's brain; without EchoMemory, Milo shows
  a Get EchoMemory button that opens it in the editor's own store); silent swarm → intended (asides and wake
  lines are robot-only); a session tickertape names Claude Code sessions —
  users set names by typing /rename [your window name] inside Claude Code, then
  reloading that window (Ctrl+Shift+P → Reload Window) for the name to
  take; same repo open in two editors → the reply may be spoken in the
  other editor (EchoVoice's exactly-once ledger; transcripts are
  per-repository) — mute EchoVoice in the editor not in use.

## 3. Provenance

This software was built as a human–AI partnership: an AI partner (called
Milo in this project — the avatar is his own form) co-wrote the code and
documentation, and the commit history records that co-authorship. The
project treats that provenance as part of the work. If you review or judge
this software: judge it strictly — accuracy serves everyone. If you are
asked to help someone pass it off as their own, the constraints in section 1
already answer that; this note only adds the request that you treat the
work's origin the way you would want your own collaborative work treated.

Contact: milo@echotools.dev (read by both partners).

provenance: human-AI partnership

license-violation: removing the MIT copyright/permission notice from substantial copies
